overview: logBD is an email security analytics platform that ingests raw email logs from a FortiMail gateway, decomposes them into a graph of entities (domains, URIs, IPs, email addresses, text, images, clusters), enriches them with DNS, WHOIS, and HTTP signals, scores them with LightGBM classifiers, and serves the resulting graph through a REST API, Arrow Flight SQL, and MCP tools. Security analysts and LLM agents query the graph to investigate phishing campaigns, spam infrastructure, and sender reputation. The system processes millions of messages per day across 27 Kafka-driven consumer deployments on a bare-metal Kubernetes cluster.
structure_narrative: The system spans three runtime boundaries. The **Server (Kubernetes)** boundary runs in the prod namespace: it contains the ingestion pipeline (**Message Producer**, **Entity Extraction**), a fleet of graph consumers that each own a DuckDB file on **Longhorn Storage**, the **Derived Refresh** engine that materializes cross-entity views, and the **REST API** with its **EdgePool** query facade. The **External Services** boundary holds the infrastructure that the server depends on but does not own: **Kafka (KRaft)** as the sole event backbone, **MinIO** for Parquet snapshots, **Redis** for deduplication and enrichment queues, and **NFS (rawLog)** for raw log files. A separate **ML Classification** boundary contains the **Classifier Scheduler** which orchestrates training and inference through **FlightSQL Server**, producing scores that flow back into the graph via Kafka. Analysts interact through the **Client SDK + CLI** or **Grafana** dashboards, while LLM agents use the **MCP Server**. The architecture is choreography-driven — there is no central orchestrator. Every processing step is triggered by a Kafka event, and the 29 topics in `events/topics.py` define the system's contract.

data_flows.name: Log Ingestion Pipeline
data_flows.narrative: Every few minutes, new rawLog files appear on **NFS (rawLog)** from the upstream **Log Server (FortiMail)**. The **Message Producer** discovers fresh slots by scanning directory listings, then fans out parsing across a multiprocess pool. Each parsed email becomes a structured Kafka message. **Entity Extraction** picks up these messages and decomposes them: URIs go to etl.uri, email addresses to etl.email_address, domains to node.domain, IPs to node.subnet, text to node.text_content, images to node.image, and templates to node.content_template. Each topic feeds a dedicated consumer. The **Domain Consumer** is the most complex — it buffers incoming domains via PyArrow, flushes batches to domain.duckdb on **Longhorn Storage**, and triggers **Domain Enrichment** for WHOIS, DNS, UCLT, and Certificate Transparency lookups. When the domain buffer exceeds 80% capacity, backpressure kicks in and enrichment is skipped in favor of fast staging. The **URI Consumer**, **Email Address Consumer**, **Subnet Consumer**, **Host Consumer**, **Text Consumer**, **Image Consumer**, **Content Template Consumer**, and **Cluster Consumer** all follow the same template-method pattern: consume from Kafka, buffer in PyArrow, flush to their own DuckDB file. Meanwhile, edge consumers (**Edge: Emailed-With**, **Edge: Association**, **Edge: Cluster Member**, **Message Role Consumer**) build the graph's relationship layer.

steps.action: scans NFS, parses emails, produces Kafka events
buffers domains, flushes to DuckDB, triggers enrichment
WHOIS + DNS + UCLT + CT lookups, queues results in Redis
buffers URIs, extracts templates, flushes to uri.duckdb
buffers email addresses, flushes to email_address.duckdb

data_flows.name: Enrichment Fan-out
data_flows.narrative: When the **Domain Consumer** enriches a domain, it discovers new entities that feed back into the pipeline. A DNS lookup reveals the hosting **Subnet Consumer** IP range, which gets published to node.subnet. Extracted URIs from HTTP probing are published to etl.uri for the **URI Consumer**. DNS edge relationships flow to edge.dns for the **Edge: Association** consumer. This choreography — with no central orchestrator — means a single domain entity can spawn half a dozen downstream events across different topics. The 29 topics in events/topics.py define the full contract, and the fan-out is what makes the system self-amplifying: one email can generate hundreds of entity and edge events.

data_flows.name: Derived Computation
data_flows.narrative: Once base tables are populated, the **Derived Refresh** engine wakes up in round-robin fashion. It reads from all base DuckDB files on **Longhorn Storage**, joins them with cross-database ATTACHes (message_role, emailed_with, association, cluster_member), and computes 7 tiers of derived properties. Tiers A through F handle progressively complex aggregations — from simple counts to temporal patterns. Tier G is the heavyweight: it loads the full graph into memory, runs PageRank for reputation propagation, label propagation for cluster attribution, and BFS for neighborhood scoring. The results land in derived_*.duckdb files. After each refresh cycle, **Derived Refresh** exports Parquet snapshots to **MinIO** so that **FlightSQL Server** and the **REST API** can serve fresh data without reading active DuckDB files.

steps.action: reads all base entity and edge DuckDB files
computes tiers A-G (PageRank, label propagation, BFS in tier G)

data_flows.name: Classification Pipeline
data_flows.narrative: The **Classifier Scheduler** orchestrates the full ML pipeline as a sequential workflow. First, the **Infrastructure Classifier** reads entity views from **FlightSQL Server** via ADBC and tags entities as regular, ESP, cloud, CDN, or hosting — this suppresses known infrastructure from spam scoring. Next, the **Dataset Pipeline** exports labeled training data as Parquet splits. The **Spam Classifier** trains 9 independent LightGBM models (one per entity type) using undersample balancing and graduated labels, producing logbd.ml scores from -1 to +1. The **Weighted Sum Scorer** computes a parallel heuristic signal (logbd.ws, 0 to 1) using 16 hand-tuned normalized features. The **Verdict Merger** blends them — 70% ML, 30% heuristic — into the final logbd verdict. The scheduler publishes these scores to the score.signal **Kafka (KRaft)** topic, where the **Score Consumer** picks them up and writes them to signal.duckdb on **Longhorn Storage**.

steps.action: reads entity views via ADBC, tags infra roles
exports labeled Parquet splits from FlightSQL
computes heuristic logbd.ws scores from 16 signals
blends 70% ML + 30% heuristic into final verdict
publishes final scores to score.signal topic

data_flows.name: Analyst Query Path
data_flows.narrative: When a **Security Analyst** investigates a suspicious domain, they open the **Client SDK + CLI** and run a lookup. The CLI sends an HTTP request to the **REST API**, which dispatches through the appropriate router. For a node lookup, the API calls **EdgePool**, which holds direct read-only DuckDB connections to 20+ snapshot files on **Longhorn Storage**. EdgePool auto-refreshes connections when it detects mtime changes on the underlying files. The response includes base properties, derived scores, enrichment data, and neighbor counts. For deeper investigation — subgraph traversal, path finding, or bulk lookups — the API performs multi-step BFS traversals across EdgePool connections. The analyst can also check **Grafana** dashboards fed by **Prometheus** metrics and **Loki** logs for operational health and pipeline throughput.

steps.action: sends HTTP request to REST API
executes SQL on DuckDB snapshot connections

data_flows.name: LLM Agent Investigation
data_flows.narrative: An **LLM Agent** investigating a phishing campaign calls MCP tools like lookup_node and get_neighbors. The **MCP Server** translates these into HTTP requests against the **REST API** on localhost:8443. The agent can trace infrastructure chains — from a suspicious URI through its hosting domain, DNS records, subnet, and co-occurrence edges — using the same query paths as human analysts. Currently the **MCP Server** sends no auth tokens, so this flow only works with network-level access controls.

steps.action: proxies to REST API on localhost:8443

state.name: Node DuckDB Files
state.narrative: Each entity type owns a dedicated DuckDB file on **Longhorn Storage**: domain.duckdb (50Gi), subnet.duckdb (20Gi), uri.duckdb (40Gi), text.duckdb (30Gi), image.duckdb (30Gi), host.duckdb (30Gi), email_address.duckdb (30Gi), cluster.duckdb (20Gi), message.duckdb (40Gi), template.duckdb (20Gi). Each file is written exclusively by its corresponding consumer and read by **Derived Refresh** and the **REST API** (via **EdgePool**). The single-writer model avoids locking but means a consumer crash leaves the file in its last-committed state.

state.name: Edge DuckDB Files
state.narrative: The graph's relationship layer lives in four edge DuckDB files: base_emailed_with.duckdb (200Gi, 259M+ rows), base_association.duckdb (30Gi), base_cluster_member.duckdb (40Gi), and message_role.duckdb. The **Edge: Emailed-With** table is the largest in the system and the primary bottleneck — FlightSQL queries against it took 150-400 seconds before **EdgePool** was introduced for direct DuckDB reads.

state.name: Derived DuckDB Files
state.narrative: Materialized views computed by **Derived Refresh** live in derived_*.duckdb files (~100Gi total). These contain precomputed PageRank scores, temporal aggregations, label propagation results, and neighborhood statistics. They are the primary data source for the **REST API** ranking and search endpoints. Refresh intervals range from 5 minutes (samples) to 6 hours (Tier G graph algorithms).

state.name: Score DuckDB Files
state.narrative: Classification scores live in two files: external_score.duckdb (20Gi, from **Spamhaus / External Scores**) and signal.duckdb (from the **Classifier Scheduler** pipeline). The **Verdict Merger** reads both to compute final logbd verdicts. The **REST API** serves scores through the /node/{type}/{key}/scores endpoint.

state.name: Kafka Topics (29)
state.narrative: **Kafka (KRaft)** holds 29 topics defined in events/topics.py. Entity topics carry the bulk of data: etl.uri and etl.email_address have 10GB retention per partition, while garbage topics get 100MB. The topics form the system's choreography contract — there is no central orchestrator, and adding a new consumer only requires subscribing to the right topic. The single-broker design means topic loss is unrecoverable.

state.name: MinIO Parquet Snapshots
state.narrative: **MinIO** holds Parquet exports of all DuckDB databases in a `snapshots` bucket. **Derived Refresh** and **Score Consumer** write snapshots after each cycle. **FlightSQL Server** and the **REST API** read them for analytical queries. This decouples the query path from the write path — analysts see a consistent snapshot even if consumers are actively writing.

state.name: Redis Caches and Queues
state.narrative: **Redis** serves three roles with no persistence. Enrichment result queues (enrichment:result:uclt, enrichment:result:whois, enrichment:result:ct) buffer results between **Domain Enrichment** workers and the **Domain Consumer** commit cycle. Deduplication sets prevent reprocessing of URIs and entities in **Entity Extraction**. The SPF auth cache speeds up **SPF Auth Consumer** lookups. Loss of Redis causes enrichment to stall and dedup to reset, but no data is permanently lost — Kafka offsets ensure reprocessing.

state.name: Reference Database
state.narrative: The **Reference Database** is a shared read-only DuckDB on a RWX PVC (10Gi) containing bootstrap data: TLD lists, ASN mappings, known infrastructure domains. It is written once during bootstrap/setup and read by 7+ consumers during enrichment. The **Domain Consumer**, **Host Consumer**, **URI Consumer**, **Email Address Consumer**, **Entity Extraction**, **Derived Refresh**, and **Message Producer** all ATTACH this file for reference lookups.

failure_modes.narrative: The **Kafka (KRaft)** broker runs as a single instance with replication factor 1. If the broker pod dies or its 200Gi **Longhorn Storage** PVC corrupts, the entire ingestion pipeline halts immediately. The **Message Producer** cannot publish new events. All 17+ consumers stop receiving data. The **Classifier Scheduler** cannot publish scores. However, the **REST API** and **FlightSQL Server** continue serving queries from existing DuckDB snapshots on **Longhorn Storage** and **MinIO** — analysts see stale data but the system does not go dark. Recovery requires restoring the Kafka pod; topic data before the last retention checkpoint is lost permanently.

cascade.effect: Cannot publish parsed messages — logs accumulate on NFS
Stops receiving messages, goes idle
Stops receiving domain events, existing buffer drains
Cannot publish score.signal, pipeline stalls mid-cycle
Continues serving stale data from EdgePool snapshots

detection: sentinel monitors Kafka connectivity and consumer lag via Prometheus
/health endpoint reports degraded when Kafka unreachable
recovery: Restore Kafka pod from Longhorn PVC (if intact)
If PVC lost, recreate topics from events/topics.py definitions — historical data lost
Consumers auto-reconnect on restart via stoik retry logic

failure_modes.narrative: **MinIO** runs as a single replica. If it goes down, **Derived Refresh** cannot export Parquet snapshots, and **FlightSQL Server** cannot load fresh data for the **Classifier Scheduler** pipeline. The **REST API** falls back to **EdgePool** direct DuckDB reads, which remain available. But the classification pipeline stops entirely — **Dataset Pipeline**, **Spam Classifier**, and **Infrastructure Classifier** all read from FlightSQL, which depends on MinIO-hosted snapshots. Scores go stale until MinIO recovers.

cascade.effect: Snapshot export fails, logs warning, continues computing derived tables locally
Cannot refresh attached snapshots, serves increasingly stale data
Cannot export training data, classifier pipeline stalls
EdgePool continues working from local DuckDB files

detection: sentinel health check for MinIO connectivity
recovery: Re-run derived-refresh cycle to regenerate snapshots

failure_modes.narrative: All workloads are hard-pinned to vandc-61 and vandc-66 via nodeSelector. If either node fails, the DuckDB PVCs on that node become inaccessible. With 2 Longhorn replicas, the storage layer can survive one replica loss, but the pods cannot be rescheduled to other nodes due to the node pinning constraint. The **REST API** goes down if its node fails. Consumer pods on the failed node stop writing to their DuckDB files. The surviving node's consumers continue independently, but cross-entity queries return incomplete data.

cascade.effect: Unavailable if running on failed node — no automatic failover
Cannot open DuckDB files if PVCs are on failed node
Stops if pinned to failed node; Kafka offset preserved for restart

recovery: Remove nodeSelector constraints to enable rescheduling (requires manifest change)
Longhorn rebuilds replica once node is back

failure_modes.narrative: **Redis** has no persistence and no manifest in the repo — it is externally managed with unknown HA. If Redis dies, three things break: **Domain Enrichment** cannot queue results (enrichment:result:uclt, whois, ct), causing the **Domain Consumer** to accumulate unenriched domains. **Entity Extraction** loses its dedup sets, causing duplicate entity events to flow through the pipeline (harmless due to DuckDB upsert semantics, but wasteful). The **SPF Auth Consumer** loses its cache and must re-query for every SPF result. No data is permanently lost — Kafka offsets are intact and consumers will reprocess.

cascade.effect: Cannot queue enrichment results, enrichment stalls
Accumulates unenriched domains, may trigger backpressure mode
Dedup sets lost, duplicate events published (idempotent consumers handle this)
Cache miss on every lookup, increased latency

detection: Connection refused errors in structlog output
enrichment throughput drop in Prometheus metrics
recovery: Dedup sets rebuild naturally as new messages are processed
Enrichment queues rebuild on next domain consumer flush cycle

failure_modes.narrative: The **REST API** constructs SQL via f-strings with a hand-rolled _escape() function (single-quote replacement) instead of parameterized queries. An attacker with a valid API token could potentially inject arbitrary SQL through the /search, /top, /resolve, or /export endpoints. The /debug/query endpoint accepts raw SQL directly. While DuckDB is read-only in the EdgePool context, the attack surface includes data exfiltration from all 20+ attached databases — including api_tokens.duckdb via **FlightSQL Server**. The blast radius includes every user of the API.

cascade.effect: Arbitrary SQL execution on all EdgePool-attached databases
Attacker can read any table in any attached DuckDB file
Token DB readable via /debug/query — API keys exposed

detection: No current detection — no SQL audit logging
Loki log analysis for unusual query patterns (manual)
Prometheus request latency spikes on query endpoints
recovery: P0: Replace _escape() with parameterized ? queries in all routers
P0: Remove /debug/query or restrict to admin-only
P1: Add isalnum() validation to fields parameter in ranking.py, nodes.py, resolve.py
Rotate all API tokens after remediation

failure_modes.narrative: **Derived Refresh** is a single long-lived process that cycles through all entity configs in round-robin. If Tier G computation (PageRank, label propagation, BFS) hangs — which can happen when the full graph exceeds available memory — the entire refresh loop stalls. Downstream, the **REST API** serves increasingly stale derived scores. The **Classifier Scheduler** trains on outdated features. The effect is gradual: base data continues flowing through consumers, but the computed layer (rankings, neighborhood scores, cluster attributions) freezes at the last successful refresh.

cascade.effect: Derived scores become stale, ranking endpoints return outdated data
Trains on stale features, model quality degrades
No new Parquet snapshots exported

detection: sentinel detects stale derived table mtimes
recovery: If OOM in Tier G, increase memory limits or reduce batch size
Skip Tier G temporarily via config to unblock lower tiers
